blocks.text: Hallucination evaluation measures how often a model generates content that is fluent and confident sounding but factually incorrect or unsupported, a failure mode that metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore, all covered in earlier topics, are largely blind to since they measure similarity, not truth.

This topic covers the different types of hallucination, the main strategies for detecting them automatically, and why this evaluation dimension needs its own dedicated approach separate from the general quality metrics covered elsewhere in this module.
1. Why Hallucination Needs Its Own Evaluation

blocks.alt: Fluent, confident output can still be factually wrong

blocks.text: A hallucinated response can be perfectly fluent, well structured, and even score reasonably on similarity metrics against a reference, while still stating something factually false, none of the metrics covered earlier in this module were designed to catch this specific failure mode directly.
2. Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Hallucination

blocks.alt: Intrinsic hallucination contradicts the source while extrinsic hallucination adds unverifiable content

blocks.text: Intrinsic hallucination directly contradicts information present in the source material the model was given, extrinsic hallucination instead adds new claims that the source neither confirms nor denies, both are problems, but intrinsic hallucination is generally considered more severe since it actively misrepresents known information.

blocks.text: 3. Checking Claims Against a Source Document

blocks.alt: A model claim is checked against the source document and marked supported or contradicted

blocks.text: When a model has access to a specific source document, part of retrieval augmented generation covered in an earlier course, hallucination detection can check each claim in the output directly against that source, flagging anything the source does not actually support.
4. Checking Claims Against External Knowledge

blocks.alt: A model claim is checked against an external knowledge base and verified or flagged

blocks.text: When no specific source document exists, hallucination detection instead checks claims against a broader external knowledge base or a separate fact-checking model, a harder problem than source-grounded checking since it requires the checking system itself to have reliable knowledge of the relevant facts.
5. Claim Extraction and Verification Pipeline

blocks.alt: Claim extraction is followed by fact verification and an aggregate score

blocks.text: A common automated approach breaks a model response into individual, checkable claims, verifies each one independently against a source or knowledge base, then aggregates the per-claim results into a single hallucination rate for the full response, a more granular and interpretable process than judging an entire response as simply hallucinated or not.
6. Human Fact-Checking vs Automated Checking

blocks.alt: Human fact checking is compared against an automated fact checking model

blocks.text: Human fact-checking remains the most reliable way to catch hallucinations, particularly subtle ones, but it is slow and expensive at scale, automated fact-checking models offer a faster, cheaper alternative that works reasonably well for catching clear-cut cases, though they can themselves make mistakes on nuanced or ambiguous claims.

blocks.title: Automated hallucination detection is itself an active research area
blocks.content: Using a language model to check another language model claims introduces its own reliability question, automated hallucination detection is generally treated as a useful filter for catching obvious cases at scale, not a fully trustworthy final judgment.

blocks.text: 7. Hallucination Rate as a Tracked Metric

Tracking hallucination rate across fine-tuning checkpoints, alongside the other metrics covered in this module, helps catch a specific and important failure mode, a model that becomes more fluent and confident sounding through training while its factual reliability actually gets worse.
8. Why High Quality Scores Do Not Rule Out Hallucination

blocks.alt: A high fluency score can still come with hallucination

blocks.text: A model can score well on fluency, ROUGE overlap, or even human evaluation ratings that focus on style and coherence, while still hallucinating specific facts, this is exactly why hallucination evaluation needs to be tracked as its own dedicated dimension rather than assumed to correlate with general quality scores.
9. Reducing Hallucination Through Fine-Tuning Choices

Fine-tuning choices covered elsewhere in this course, grounding training data in verified sources, penalizing unsupported claims during preference optimization, both covered in earlier modules, can directly reduce hallucination rate, making this evaluation dimension not just a diagnostic tool but a target that training decisions can be optimized against.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a document summarization model runs a claim extraction and verification pipeline against their evaluation set, comparing each generated summary claim against the original source document.

They find an intrinsic hallucination rate of twelve percent, summaries contradicting specific numbers or names present in the source, a problem their ROUGE scores, tracking word overlap rather than factual accuracy, had entirely missed, prompting a targeted fine-tuning adjustment that penalizes source-contradicting claims specifically, which measurably reduces the hallucination rate on a follow up evaluation run.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a model with strong ROUGE or fluency scores must also have a low hallucination rate
Not distinguishing intrinsic hallucinations, which contradict a given source, from the generally less severe extrinsic ones
Relying entirely on automated fact-checking without any human spot-checking of ambiguous cases
Only checking hallucination rate once before deployment instead of tracking it across fine-tuning checkpoints

blocks.text: Practice

Take a short source paragraph and write two model style summaries of it, one that stays fully accurate to the source and one that includes a subtle factual contradiction, then reason through how a claim extraction and verification pipeline would need to work to catch that specific contradiction.
Key Takeaway

Hallucination evaluation specifically targets fluent but factually incorrect or unsupported content, a failure mode general similarity and fluency metrics cannot catch, using claim extraction and verification against a source document or external knowledge base to produce a hallucination rate that should be tracked as its own dedicated dimension throughout fine-tuning.
